title: Political Contexts and Digital Ecosystems
summary: How algorithms, memes and the attention economy shape political reality, and how to use video activism without getting played by it.
description: This lesson takes a deep look at how political, social and civic life has changed in the age of digital platforms. Society has become "extremely online" across all generations. The lesson introduces "brain rot" (Oxford Word of the Year 2024) to describe minds overwhelmed by algorithmic content.

It traces how digital spaces evolved from the text-based networks of 2010 to the video-dominated landscape of 2025. It frames this shift as a return to an "oral culture", where social videos are the new storytelling campfires.
Participants examine how physical political spaces (youth culture, social centres and squats of the 80s and 90s) have been replaced by digital ones like Discord, Twitch, Reddit and Fortnite.

The lesson covers the dangers of "technofeudalism" (platforms as modern feudal estates) and of "clicktivism" and "slacktivism". It shows how radicalisation works under the hood: memes act as Trojan horses for ideology, and irony and "shitposting" shift the Overton window.

Finally, it unpacks the algorithmic attention economy, rooted in Facebook's 2009 introduction of the algorithmic feed (the internet's "original sin"). It gives participants the psychological and technical strategies of effective video activism.
objectives: Identify how the attention economy works and how algorithms shape political reality
Analyse how humour and "shitposting" carry ideological radicalisation
Understand the shift from physical to digital political spaces (Discord, Twitch, TikTok…)
Weigh clicktivism against tangible political action
Apply the principles of video activism (3-second rule, metrics, emotional hooks) responsibly
targetGroup: Young people interested in media literacy, digital sociology and activism, especially those active online who want to understand the mechanics behind the content they consume and create.

outcomes.outcome: Explain the impact of the digital attention economy
outcomes.content: Attention economy; algorithms as "black boxes"; the role of "brain rot"
outcomes.methods: Short lecture; visual analysis of social media feeds

outcomes.outcome: Identify ideological tools in digital media
outcomes.content: Memes as "Trojan horses"; shitposting; shifting the Overton window
outcomes.methods: Guided analysis of case studies (memes, videos)

outcomes.content: Clicktivism vs. real-world impact; video activism; psychological triggers
outcomes.methods: Case study of successful vs. failed digital campaigns

steps.title: Digital daily life
bullets: Discussion of "brain rot" and the move from text-based to video-saturated environments.
prompts: How has the way you consume information changed over the last few years?

steps.title: The political digital ecosystem
bullets: **New political spaces:** Discord, Twitch and Reddit as the new "town squares".
**Ideological funnels:** how memes act as Trojan horses for radicalisation and shift the Overton window.

steps.title: Workshop: the anatomy of a viral message
bullets: Focus on the **3-second rule**, pacing and emotional triggers: laughter, anger, belonging.
Case study: why do we share what we share? Identity building vs. community belonging.

activity.intro: Groups analyse a current viral video or political meme. They identify:

steps.title: The intended emotion
steps.text: What is the content trying to make you feel?

steps.title: The hidden message
steps.text: Is there an ideological message underneath, if any?

steps.title: The algorithmic boost
steps.text: How did the algorithm likely push this content?

steps.title: Reflection and closing
prompts: How can we stay critical in a digital-feudal ecosystem?
Can we use these platforms for good without falling into slacktivism?
steps.keyMessage: Each participant shares one strategy for being more mindful of algorithmic influence.

materials.name: A selection of current TikTok/Reels political content
"Anatomy of an Algorithmic Post": deconstruction template
Laptop, projector, internet connection and personal devices for quick research

evaluation: Active participation in the group analysis, the quality of insights in the worksheets, and a final oral reflection on media responsibility.
